editorial.headline: Tofu, Tempe and Oncom Retail: Nationally Open, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This specialised food retail activity is open to full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium makes registration unavailable on the island today.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register this activity in Bali today. That is the practical starting point for a business focused on retail sales of tofu, tempe, tauco and oncom: national PMA openness does not override the province-wide Bali restriction. The distinction is decisive. It is the fact that should govern any initial decision about Bali. This code is defined narrowly by the products sold, but its registration outcome turns on two distinct regulatory settings.

At its core, the activity is specialised retail trade in tofu, tempe, tauco and oncom. The named products are not decorative examples; they are the stated focus of the retail scope. It is available at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. That range gives it a formal place across every named business scale, while keeping the activity anchored in a specific retail offering rather than a broad trading label. The scope makes no claim beyond that specialised retail function. The activity therefore sets the business identity before the ownership and location questions arise. A Micro-scale or Large-scale enterprise can sit within the stated scale range, provided its declared business is this specialised retail trade.

At the national level, the code is open (TERBUKA) to PMA and has a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In plain terms, national rules permit full foreign ownership for PMA registration. The record sources that national setting to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Its 100% ceiling is national, not a Bali-side ownership allowance. National openness is meaningful, but it is not a portability guarantee: it identifies what is open nationally rather than deciding the separate Bali position.

Bali reaches a different result. At Large scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, placing the activity within Bali's moratorium. The provincial rule blocks PMA for all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI island-wide and permanently, and the record marks this activity as blocked. The stated moratorium is dated May 13, 2026. The national ceiling and Bali position are not competing figures: the national ceiling remains 100%, while the Bali outcome is a registration block created by the moratorium. For a foreign-owned vehicle considering Bali, the conclusion is direct: it cannot register this activity there today despite national openness.
